title: S&P Global domain -- financial data, pipeline architecture
exp: Understanding what S&P Global does and what fundamentals data means lets you give concrete contextualised answers. The architecture questions are directly about the pipeline in the JD.
pts: S&P Global provides financial data, analytics, ratings, and platforms to financial institutions.
Fundamentals data: revenue, EBITDA, EPS, P/E ratio, debt levels from company filings (10-K, 10-Q). Used for valuation.
Market data: real-time/historical prices. Different from fundamentals -- changes millisecond vs quarterly.
The 50-source pipeline: each provider has its own schema, delivery mechanism, and quirks.
Config-driven ingestion: each source is metadata, not hardcoded logic. Adding source 51 is a config entry.
Data quality matters -- wrong data affects trading decisions. Dead-letter queues and validation alerts are non-negotiable.
Idempotency: re-running on the same data produces the same result -- mode('overwrite') for safe reruns.

viz.cap: 50-source S&P pipeline -- each layer separately scalable and observable

qa.q: Design a pipeline ingesting fundamentals from 50 sources daily, serving batch analytics and a near-real-time dashboard.
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Three layers: (1) Ingestion -- NiFi fetches data and lands raw files in S3, config-driven per source. (2) Processing -- Spark validates types and business rules; invalid records go to dead-letter S3 with alerts; valid records become Parquet partitioned by date. (3) Serving -- Spark batch jobs query processed data for full analytics; pre-aggregated daily rollups feed the dashboard so it does not hit the heavy pipeline on every page load.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** EF Core builds an Expression Tree, translates it via the relational SQL provider into a parameterized T-SQL query, and materializes entities into the DbContext Change Tracker. N+1 queries occur when navigating un-included navigation properties in a loop.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing queries without AsNoTracking() in read-only APIs forces EF Core to keep snapshot copies of all returned entities in memory, causing high RAM usage and CPU tracking overhead.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** AsNoTracking() speeds up read queries by 20-30% and reduces memory footprint, but disables identity resolution and automatic change tracking for updates.

qa.q: How do you design so adding source 51 doesn't require a code change?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Config-driven: store per-source metadata in a config table (DynamoDB or S3 JSON) -- URL, auth, format, schema, validation rules, schedule. The ingestion code reads this at runtime and operates generically. Adding source 51 is adding a config row. Zero code changes, zero deploy.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transient creates a new instance on every request; Scoped creates one instance per HTTP request container; Singleton lives for the app domain lifespan. Capturing a Scoped service inside a Singleton captures the DbContext across requests, causing concurrency bugs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Instantiating new HttpClient() instances manually causes socket exhaustion in OS TIME_WAIT state under high concurrency. Fix: register typed clients with IHttpClientFactory to manage handler lifetimes and DNS refresh.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** IHttpClientFactory prevents socket leaks and manages DNS rotation, but requires explicit Polly retry and circuit breaker policies to prevent cascade failures during downstream outages.

qa.q: What is idempotency and why is it essential?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** An idempotent pipeline produces the same result regardless of how many times it runs on the same input. Re-running today's pipeline should not duplicate records. Implement via mode('overwrite') on Parquet partitions, MERGE statements in SQL, date-partitioned output paths. Enables safe reruns -- how you fix bugs without corrupting data.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Async methods compile into an IAsyncStateMachine struct managed by the AsyncMethodBuilder. Awaiting an uncompleted task yields execution back to the caller. Blocking with .Result on a thread bound to a SynchronizationContext causes deadlocks when the continuation waits for the blocked thread.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Sync-over-async (.Result or .Wait()) on ASP.NET request threads rapidly exhausts thread pool threads, leading to HTTP 503 gateway timeouts and request queuing under load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Async all the way preserves thread pool scalability, but requires passing CancellationToken through all layers and avoiding sync blocking methods everywhere.
